prompt: Architectural night photograph, front entrance seen from the driveway at blue hour. An unbranded matte video doorbell camera with a brushed-steel faceplate is mounted on the painted-wood trim of a deep pine green front door, placed off-centre on the left third. Warm ochre light from the hallway inside spills through the sidelight beside it, catching a soft rim highlight on the camera's lens ring; that interior glow is the only warm light against a deep graphite-blue dusk. Bone-white trim, clean stucco wall falling into shadow, crisp night air. 35mm lens at f/2.8 with gentle edge falloff, deep focus on the door plane, long-exposure calm, fine film grain, no people, no text, no logos.

rationale: The protagonist is a machine at the home's threshold — the doorbell camera — and architectural_night places it in its true narrative context: the front door at dusk, where lit windows are the only warm light, mirroring the story's point that the conversation now runs on the home's own network rather than a distant cloud. The blue-hour calm with the small camera as focal anchor gives cover-grade atmosphere without stock datacenter clichés, and the treatment has not appeared in the last four headers.
cue: Your Doorbell Won't Need the Cloud
subject: an unbranded video doorbell camera mounted on painted-wood trim beside a front door at blue hour, its lens ring catching warm hallway light through the sidelight
core_thesis: Home Assistant 2026.11 made Matter 1.5 cameras first-class devices with two-way talk, so the doorbell conversation vendors fold into subscriptions now runs entirely on your own network.
core_conflict: vendor cloud plans that relayed video and carried your voice back to the door versus a direct browser-to-camera WebRTC stream hosted on the homeowner's own hub and network.
composition: tight exterior three-quarter view at eye level, the doorbell camera commanding the left third of the door trim, deep blue dusk wall and unlit porch filling the right two-thirds as editorial negative space
